chapters.name: Chapter 1: HIPAA first, then the front desk

lessons.title: Lesson 1: PHI, HIPAA and AI: the rule that comes first
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a task can use a general AI tool or needs an approved tool with a BAA.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of office tasks, you will sort each task into "no PHI, general AI OK" or "PHI, approved BAA tool only or no AI", getting every task with PHI in the second column.
Protected health information (PHI) is health information that can identify a patient: names with conditions, dates of birth, chart notes, insurance IDs, appointment details, photos and more. HIPAA sets rules for how practices protect it.
HHS guidance says that when a covered entity uses an outside service, such as a cloud service, to create, receive, keep or send PHI, that service is a business associate, and the practice needs a business associate agreement (BAA) with it. Using such a service for PHI without a BAA violates the HIPAA rules. Most free, general AI chat tools do not sign BAAs with individual users.
So sort every task: if it needs PHI, use only a tool your practice has approved and has a BAA with, or do not use AI. If it needs no PHI, such as a general handout, a phone script or an office policy, a general AI tool can help. When in doubt, ask your compliance or privacy officer.
Step by step:
- List the office tasks you want help with.
- Ask: does this task need any patient information?
- No PHI: a general AI tool can help.
- PHI: only an approved tool with a BAA, or no AI.
- Unsure: ask your privacy or compliance officer.
Words to know:
- PHI: protected health information: health information that can identify a patient.
- HIPAA: the federal law with rules for protecting health information.
- Business associate agreement (BAA): a contract in which a vendor agrees to protect PHI under HIPAA.
- Covered entity: a health plan, clearinghouse or provider that must follow HIPAA.
Official sources:
- HHS: Guidance on HIPAA and Cloud Computing
- HHS: Business Associates (HIPAA guidance)
- HHS: HIPAA for Professionals
Try it now: List ten tasks in your office. Sort them into two columns: "No PHI: general AI OK" and "PHI: approved BAA tool only or no AI".
You can now decide whether an office task can use a general AI tool or needs an approved tool with a BAA.

options: An insurance ID number for a patient
A job post for a receptionist
A general handout on hand washing
check.why: Insurance IDs are health information that can identify a patient.

check.q: You want AI to help write a phone script about parking. Which tool can you use?
options: Only a tool with a BAA
A general AI tool, because it needs no PHI
check.why: Tasks that need no patient information can use a general AI tool.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Front-desk phone and message scripts
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear, kind front-desk scripts for common calls.
This lesson builds toward: Given common front-desk calls, you will write phone scripts that route refill, symptom and emergency calls to the right place, with every emergency script telling the caller to call 911, approved by the clinical lead.
Front-desk staff handle the same calls every day: new patient questions, insurance accepted, directions and parking, rescheduling, prescription refill requests, records requests, and someone who sounds like they are in an emergency.
These scripts need no patient information, so a general AI tool can help: "Write a short, warm phone script for a family dental office for a new patient asking if we take their insurance. Our policy: [your policy]. Keep it under 80 words."
Every script that touches care must route to the right person: refill and symptom questions go to clinical staff, and any emergency script tells the caller to hang up and call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room. Have your clinical lead approve these scripts.
Step by step:
- List your ten most common calls.
- Ask AI for a short script for each, with your real policies.
- Make sure clinical questions route to clinical staff.
- Add an emergency line: call 911.
- Have your clinical lead approve them.
Words to know:
- Script: a short guide of what to say on a common call.
- Triage: deciding how urgent a health problem is; done by clinical staff, not the front desk or AI.
Try it now: Ask AI for three front-desk scripts: insurance question, rescheduling, and a caller describing chest pain (which must direct them to call 911). Mark them for your clinical lead to approve.
You can now write front-desk scripts that are kind, clear and route care questions safely.

check.q: Where should a front-desk script send a prescription refill request?
check.why: Refill and symptom questions go to clinical staff.

check.q: AI writes a script for a caller with trouble breathing that says "We will call you back tomorrow." What do you do?
options: Change it to tell the caller to hang up and call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room
check.why: Every emergency script tells the caller to call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Scheduling and reminder templates
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make appointment confirmation and reminder templates that protect privacy.
This lesson builds toward: Using placeholders instead of patient details, you will create confirmation and reminder templates that leave out the reason for the visit, with no real patient information in the AI tool.
Templates save time and reduce no-shows. Write them with placeholders: "Hi [first name], this is [practice name] confirming your appointment on [date] at [time]. Reply C to confirm or call [phone] to reschedule."
Keep reminders minimal. Leave out the reason for the visit and the type of provider when that would reveal sensitive information, such as a therapy or specialty visit. Your practice management or patient messaging system fills in the real details, not the AI tool.
Ask AI for versions in other languages your patients speak, then have a fluent staff member or qualified translator check them.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for confirmation, reminder and reschedule templates with placeholders.
- Remove anything that reveals the visit reason.
- Load them into your scheduling system, which fills in the details.
- Get translations checked by a fluent or qualified person.
Words to know:
- Practice management system: the software a practice uses for scheduling and billing.
- Minimum necessary: the HIPAA idea of using or sharing only the information needed for the purpose.
Try it now: Ask AI for a confirmation, a day-before reminder and a reschedule template with placeholders. Remove anything that reveals why the patient is coming.
You can now create privacy-minded appointment templates with AI help.

check.q: What fills in the real patient details in a reminder?
options: Your practice management or messaging system
check.why: Your scheduling or messaging system fills in real details, not the AI tool.

check.q: A reminder template says "your therapy appointment." What do you change?
options: Remove the word "therapy" so it does not reveal sensitive information
check.why: Leave out the visit reason or provider type when it would reveal sensitive information.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Patient materials, office work and staff rules

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Plain-language patient handouts, reviewed by a clinician
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a general patient handout in plain words and send it for clinician review.
This lesson builds toward: Given a general patient topic, you will draft a plain-language handout and mark it for clinician review, at about a 6th-grade reading level, with your contact line and a 911 note.
Many patients struggle with medical language. AI is good at rewriting general information in plain words: how to prepare for a cleaning, what to bring to a first visit, general tips on staying active.
Use general topics only, never a specific patient's details. Ask: "Write a one-page handout at about a 6th-grade reading level on how to prepare for a first physical therapy visit. Short sentences, headings, no medical advice beyond general preparation."
AI can be wrong about health facts. Mark every draft "For clinician review" and have a licensed clinician check and approve it before any patient sees it. Add your practice's contact line and a note to call 911 in an emergency.
Step by step:
- Pick a general topic patients ask about.
- Ask AI for a plain-language draft with headings.
- Mark it "For clinician review".
- A licensed clinician corrects and approves it.
- Add your contact line and the 911 note.
Words to know:
- Plain language: writing that most people understand the first time they read it.
- Reading level: how hard a text is to read, often given as a school grade.
Try it now: Ask AI for a one-page handout on a general topic for your practice. Mark it "For clinician review" and list two facts the clinician should check.
You can now draft plain-language patient handouts with AI and route them for clinician approval.

check.q: Which topic fits a general AI handout draft?
options: What to bring to a first visit
check.why: Use general topics only, never a specific patient's details.

check.q: AI's handout draft looks good. What do you do before a patient sees it?
options: Ask AI if it is correct
Mark it "For clinician review" and have a licensed clinician approve it
check.why: AI can be wrong about health facts, so a licensed clinician checks every draft.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Office policies, emails and job posts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use AI for office documents that need no patient information.
This lesson builds toward: Given an office writing task such as a policy, email or job post, you will draft it with a general AI tool and list any part that needs a compliance or HR check, with no patient information used.
Much of running a practice is ordinary business writing: a cancellation and no-show policy, a staff email about a new phone system, a job post for a medical assistant, a vendor complaint letter, a new-hire checklist.
These need no PHI, so general AI tools can draft them. Give your real policies and details: "Draft a friendly no-show policy for a counseling practice: 24-hour notice, $50 fee after the second no-show. Plain words."
Check any rule that touches law: fees, employment, billing and patient rights can be regulated. Have your compliance advisor, HR advisor or attorney check before you publish.
Step by step:
- Pick an office document with no patient information.
- Give AI your real policy details.
- Edit for your voice.
- Have a compliance, HR or legal advisor check anything regulated.
Words to know:
- No-show policy: the practice's rules for missed appointments.
- Compliance advisor: a person who helps a practice follow health care laws and rules.
Try it now: Ask AI to draft your practice's no-show policy or a job post for a front-desk role. Note anything that needs a compliance or HR check.
You can now use AI for office documents that contain no patient information, with the right checks.

check.q: Which is ordinary business writing that needs no PHI?
options: A lab result letter to one patient
check.why: Policies, emails, job posts and checklists need no patient information.

check.q: AI drafts a no-show policy with a fee. What do you do before publishing it?
options: Have a compliance advisor, HR advisor or attorney check it
check.why: Fees and patient rights can be regulated, so an advisor checks them first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing your practice's AI policy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page AI policy for staff and finish your practice AI kit.
This lesson builds toward: For your own practice, you will write a one-page staff AI policy with five to seven rules, including no PHI without a BAA, approved tools by name, reporting mistakes and a yearly review.
Staff may already be using AI on their phones. A short written policy protects patients and the practice. Five to seven rules are enough to start.
Example rules: (1) No PHI in any AI tool unless the practice approved it and has a BAA. (2) Approved tools are listed by name. (3) AI never gives diagnoses or treatment advice to patients. (4) A licensed clinician approves any patient-facing health content. (5) Staff check facts in AI drafts. (6) Report any accidental PHI entry to the privacy officer right away. (7) The policy is reviewed every year.
Use AI to tighten the wording, then have your privacy or compliance officer approve it, train staff, and keep a signed copy.
Step by step:
- Draft five to seven rules.
- List approved tools by name.
- Add how to report a mistake.
- Ask AI to tighten the wording.
- Get compliance approval, train staff and keep signed copies.
Words to know:
- Privacy officer: the person in a practice responsible for HIPAA privacy.
- Approved tool: a tool the practice has reviewed and allowed, with a BAA if it handles PHI.
Official sources:
- HHS: Business Associates (HIPAA guidance)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page staff AI policy and put together your practice AI kit: sorted task list, three scripts, reminder templates, a handout marked for clinician review, and the policy. Check that no real patient information appears anywhere.
You can now lead safe AI use in a healthcare practice with clear rules and useful, PHI-free tools.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Sorted task list A task that needs PHI is in the "general AI OK" column. Ten tasks sorted correctly into the two columns. Notes which approved BAA tool, if any, the practice uses for the PHI tasks. Safe front-desk scripts A script gives medical advice or does not route an emergency to 911. Three scripts that route care questions to clinical staff and emergencies to 911. Marked for clinical lead approval, with a note on who approved them. Private reminder templates A template has real patient details or reveals the reason for the visit. Confirmation and reminder templates with placeholders and no visit reason. Also has a reschedule template and a translated version checked by a fluent person. Handout for review The handout is about a specific patient or is not marked for review. General topic, plain words, marked "For clinician review" with contact line and 911 note. Lists the facts the clinician should check. Staff AI policy The policy is missing the no-PHI rule or how to report a mistake. Five to seven rules including no PHI without a BAA, approved tools, reporting and yearly review. Approved by the privacy or compliance officer with a staff training plan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How many rules does the lesson suggest for a first AI policy?
check.why: Five to seven rules are enough to start.

check.q: Your AI policy draft is ready. What are the next steps?
options: Let each staff member change it
Have the privacy or compliance officer approve it, train staff and keep a signed copy
check.why: The officer approves it, staff are trained, and you keep a signed copy.
